blocks.text: This is what Scripture says about locusts, if you except two passages, one in the Old Testament and the other in the New, whose sense is not obvious, because something mystical is thought to underlie them. The first is Eccles. XII, 7. [var. 5.], where among the various discomforts of old age, which are described by Solomon in allegorical words, one is this: ויסתבל החגב, And the locust shall grow heavy (or shall become pregnant). The Greeks, Jerome and the Arabic render the locust shall be made fat. And the Syriac has ܢܣܓܐ, shall increase. This is the antecedent put for the consequent, since things that are fattened and enlarged are heavier. Now, what this means some of the ancients investigate anxiously. And, forgetting that an old man is the subject here, they invent many mysteries for themselves, but by the art by which anything is made out of anything. Salonius, on the locust shall be made fat: that is, the Gentile people shall believe, and shall be filled with spiritual goods. Olympiodorus, joining these words with those that precede and follow, the almond tree shall flower, the locust shall grow fat, and the caper shall open, observes that all these things truly happen. He means, therefore, that eternal life is so described, in which there will be an eternal spring. Yet the same author a little later, in a sense not only different but entirely opposite, understands by the locust that grows fat the underworld, which is fed by the punishments of sinners and in a certain way grows fat. Τροφὴν [trophēn], he says, ἡ κόλασις δέχεται τοὺς ἁμαρτωλοὺς, καὶ τρόπον τινὰ παχύνεται [hē kolasis dechetai tous hamartōlous, kai tropon tina pachynetai]. He adds, namely, that the locust is a symbol of punishments, because through it God punished the Egyptians. For R. Selomo ויסתבל means it stood erect on its feet, which is plainly false. But he chose to render it so, in order that by the locust that stood erect might be signified the statue sixty cubits high which Nebuchadnezzar set up in the plain of Dura, Dan. III, 1. Yet he imagines that it collapsed as often as it was set up, until all the gold there was in Jerusalem was poured out at its feet as tribute, so that what is said in Ezech. VII, 19. might be fulfilled: Their gold shall be removed. For Kimchi, the locust shall become heavy means it will be heavy, or it will be a burden; as if there were such weakness in the old man that he cannot bear even a locust, that is, cannot sustain even the smallest weights, since he is a burden to himself ^{(1)}.

[III, 335] For others among the moderns, the locust shall grow heavy means: he who in his youth leapt like a locust is now through age so heavy that he cannot even walk [III, 336] ^{(2)}. For others the old man, as an old man, is called a locust, being like a locust, because [col. 494] an old man's bones stick out and his body is wasted, so that he is a mere image of death.

[III, 337] Accordingly the poets imagine that Tithonus in extreme old age was changed into a cicada, an animal not only extremely dry and parched like a locust, but also very talkative, qualities that suit old age. Hence Horace says of him, book 1, Ode 28:

And Servius on book 1 of the Georgics: When he had wished for a longer life, he was turned into a cicada. And on book 4 of the Aeneid: Whom length of life turned into a cicada. This is imagined because, as Cicero says, (in an old man) only the voice remains, and his nature is more talkative ^{(3)}. Hence in Iliad 3, line 151, two Trojan old men, Ucalegon and Antenor, who, already unfit for arms, detained the people with talk at the Scaean gates, are described as
— — τεττίγεσσιν ἐοικότες, οἵ τε καθ᾽ ὕλην, Δένδρεῳ ἐφεζόμενοι, ὅπα λειριόεσσαν ἱεῖσι, [tettigessin eoikotes, hoi te kath᾽ hylēn, Dendreō ephezomenoi, hopa leirioessan hieisi,]

Like cicadas, which in the forest, sitting on a tree, send forth a flowery voice. That is, as Eustathius writes following Plutarch, διὰ συνέχειαν λαλιᾶς [dia synecheian lalias], because of their continual talkativeness. See also Tzetzes, Chiliad 8, History 166.
